name: Type Safety Best Practices
description: This module captures the best practices for type safety, distilled from common failure modes and what tends to hold up over time.
content:
This module captures the best practices for type safety, distilled from common failure modes and what tends to hold up over time.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Validate type safety outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
2. Surface known limitations of a chosen type safety approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
3. When type safety decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
4. Document any non-obvious type safety decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
5. State assumptions about type safety explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
6. Measure before optimizing any type safety bottleneck; do not guess at what is slow.
7. Re-check edge cases relevant to type safety (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
8. Before starting type safety work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
9. When multiple type safety strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
10. Keep type safety changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.
11. Keep type safety outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not skip documenting type safety assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Avoid introducing new type safety abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of type safety correctness.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for type safety, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
